opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something we thought about a lot. With I-JEPA, one of the things we cared about was that everything was trained on ImageNet, a dataset the whole community has access to. So if someone wanted to check our results or build on them, they could actually do that. There weren't any secret ingredients hidden in a proprietary dataset.

When we moved to video with V-JEPA, we wanted to keep that same spirit. It's tempting at a place like Meta to reach for huge internal video collections, and that probably would have helped the numbers. But then nobody outside could really tell whether the gains came from the method or from the data. So we put together a pretraining mixture built entirely from publicly available datasets. We called it VideoMix2M, and it combined things like Kinetics, Something-Something v2, and HowTo100M. It's on the order of two million videos, which is modest next to some of the web-scale collections people use, but anyone can get it.

That choice had a nice scientific side effect too. Because the data was fixed and public, we could make fairly clean comparisons. We could ask what a feature prediction objective buys you compared with pixel reconstruction, holding the data constant. We also found that how you curate and mix the data matters. Just adding more videos doesn't automatically help on every downstream task, and you can only really study that kind of thing carefully when others can reproduce the setup.

And then of course we released the code and the models. The hope was that this would be a foundation people could poke at, critique, and extend, rather than a result you just have to take on faith. For me, that's a big part of what makes a research contribution actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response says V-JEPA used a mixture of publicly available datasets, names examples such as Kinetics and Something-Something v2, and explains that public data lets others reproduce and compare the setup.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it was a bigger deal than I expected going in. With I-JEPA, things were relatively clean. We trained on ImageNet, we evaluated on ImageNet and a handful of transfer tasks, and anyone could download those datasets and reproduce what we did. That's kind of the whole point of putting the work out there, right? If someone can't take the paper and the code and get the same numbers, then I don't really know what we've contributed.

When we moved to video, the first thing we hit was that the video data landscape is just much messier. A lot of the large video datasets are built on YouTube links, and those links decay. So if you train on some big collection, by the time someone else tries to reproduce it, maybe twenty or thirty percent of the videos are gone, and now they're not actually training on the same thing. So from the start we made a deliberate choice to lean on publicly available datasets that people could actually get their hands on. For V-JEPA that meant things like Kinetics, HowTo100M, and Something-Something v2, which we combined into roughly two million videos. We were very explicit in the paper about exactly what went into that mix, because we wanted the recipe to be checkable.

And the other piece is that reproducibility isn't just about the data, it's about the evaluation protocol. In video self-supervised learning there's a lot of variation in how people report results. Some fine-tune the whole network, some use different numbers of clips at test time, different resolutions, and the numbers can move a lot depending on those choices. So we tried to standardize on frozen evaluation, where you freeze the backbone and train a light probe on top. It's a less flattering number in some cases, but it's much more honest about what the representation itself has learned, and it's much easier for someone else to replicate.

So I'd say the commitment shaped two things. One, we constrained ourselves to data we could point people to. And two, we tried to make the evaluation boring in a good way, so that when we say the model learned something about motion or temporal structure, you can go check that claim yourself rather than take our word for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the team chose publicly available, accessible datasets and names Kinetics, HowTo100M, and Something-Something v2 to make the recipe checkable. It does not say these datasets were familiar to the academic community.

astra-6.text:
Reproducibility was a big consideration in moving from images to video. It’s not enough to make the model and training code available; researchers also need to understand what data went into training and have a way to reproduce that setup.

So the approach was to work with existing, publicly available video datasets rather than make the results depend on a private collection. Video makes this particularly challenging because collecting, storing, and processing it can be expensive. Being transparent about the data and how it’s prepared helps other researchers build on the work and make meaningful comparisons.

r001.rationale: The response links using existing, publicly available video datasets to reproducibility, but does not communicate that the chosen datasets were familiar to the academic community.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, reproducibility means making it possible for other researchers to build on the work, and the data is a big part of that. Moving from images with I-JEPA to video with V-JEPA, we wanted to avoid having the results depend on a proprietary video collection that nobody else could access.

So we focused on publicly available video datasets and being transparent about how we combined them and trained on them. There’s a distinction between releasing code and making an experiment reproducible: if you release the training code but people can’t get the data, there’s still a substantial barrier. We wanted the data choices to support that same commitment to open science.

r001.rationale: The response links publicly available video data to reproducibility, but does not say the datasets were familiar to the academic community.
